q: In Grade 10, one dimensional motion such as linear motion and free fall motion was studied.
e: This is a direct statement from the textbook introducing the progression from one-dimensional to two-dimensional motion.

q: Two-dimensional motion is the simplest type of motion which can be encountered in many cases.
e: One dimensional motion, not two-dimensional motion, is the simplest type of motion.

q: In two-dimensional motion, the object may move in both the x and y direction simultaneously.
e: Two-dimensional motion involves simultaneous movement in both the x and y directions.

q: In order to describe the motion of an object in two dimensions, scalar concept must be used.
e: Vector concept, not scalar concept, must be used to describe two-dimensional motion.

q: The displacement vector of the object from P to Q is $\Delta \vec{r}$.
e: The displacement vector representing the change in position from point P to Q is denoted as $\Delta \vec{r}$.

q: The perpendicular components of $\Delta \vec{r}$ are $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$.
e: The displacement vector $\Delta \vec{r}$ can be resolved into perpendicular x and y components, $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$.

q: The magnitude of $\Delta \vec{r}$ is given by $\Delta r = \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2 - (\Delta y)^2}$.
e: The magnitude is given by the Pythagorean theorem: $\Delta r = \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2}$.

q: To find the direction of $\Delta \vec{r}$, the formula $\tan \theta = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ is used.
e: The angle $\theta$ of the displacement vector is determined using the ratio of its y-component to its x-component.

q: Instantaneous velocity is given by $\vec{v} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t}$.
e: Instantaneous velocity is the limit of the average velocity as the time interval approaches zero.

q: Average acceleration is given by $\vec{a}_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}$.
e: Average acceleration is defined as the change in velocity divided by the time taken.

q: Instantaneous acceleration is given by $\vec{a} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}$.
e: Instantaneous acceleration is the limit of average acceleration as the time interval approaches zero.

q: An object moving with constant speed along a curved path is not accelerating.
e: An object moving with constant speed along a curved path is accelerating because the direction of its velocity is changing.

q: The direction of the velocity of an object moving along a curved path is tangential to its path.
e: At any point on a curved path, the velocity vector is directed tangentially to the path.

q: An object is accelerated whenever the velocity changes in magnitude, direction, or both.
e: Acceleration occurs with any change in the velocity vector, whether in magnitude, direction, or both.
